utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls B-179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While the witness is coming, Mr. Groome, one minor housekeeping matter. We had handed in on Friday directive number 7 concerning Srebrenica. I understand that that will formally be produced in due course. I think it's really rather early to produce it at the moment, so it may be that we'll just simply hand it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we are having problems with the -- this distorted microphone, as you know, with leakage, so we must make sure that witnesses understand that they should not speak early, and perhaps you could try and instil that in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will remind the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder of 13 exhibits to be used with this witness. Could I ask that a number be assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we could give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 539, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like now to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, before I begin my examination of you, I would like to remind you of the following: Part of the protections extended to you by the Chamber are -- is a distortion of your voice. In order for that to be effective, it's very important that you watch the person asking you questions and make sure that this little red light on the top of their microphone is off when you answer the question. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we can begin by asking you to take a look at Exhibit 539, tab 1. My first question to you is: Is that your name on the top of that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last line on that page, does that indicate the position that you held that's relevant to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe in a sentence or two what was the Association of Emigrant Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The Association of Serbs and Emigrants of Serbia was an organisation for aid to Serbs outside Serbia, actually, in the diaspora. It worked on humanitarian aid and providing supplies for the battlefields of Croatia and Bosnia. It also transported humanitarian and military supplies and aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did there come a time when the name was changed of that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. The Association of Serbs was originally called the Association of Emigrants of Serbia. Later, the name changed to the Association of Serbs and Emigrants of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you to talk about your testimony in detail, I'm going to ask you the names of four people, and if I could ask you, in simply a sentence, identify the position that each of these people held. The first person I'd like to ask you about is a person by the name of Branislav Crnjevic -- Crncevic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Brana Crncevic was the president of the Association of Serbs and Emigrants of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe what, if anything, you know about his relationship to the accused, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that in those days they were good friends, and I know that Brana often went to see Mr. Milosevic. On one occasion, I myself drove him in my car to the house of Mr. Milosevic. In front of the house I dropped him off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The person by the name of Milan Prodanic. Can you tell us briefly who he was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Milan Prodanic was the head of the 6th department of the state security department of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What can you tell us about his relationship to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: He was directly subordinated to Jovica Stanisic, and they were in permanent contact. They discussed the work and supplies issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And a person by the name of Lieutenant Colonel Bora Stanisic. Can you tell us what you know about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Bora Stanisic was in the command of the town military post 5055 and was in charge of the military warehouses in Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you aware of any family relationship between Bora Stanisic and Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I don't know that they were in any kind of family relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last person I'd like to ask you about is Mr. Tepavcevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I met Mr. Tepavcevic only once in the MUP of Serbia. He was to have worked with Bora Stanisic before even Prodanic, but they didn't get on for some reason, and so he didn't work with Tepavcevic but with Milan Prodanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness approach the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to sit up a little bit closer to the microphone so that it may pick up your voice a bit more clearer. During the course of my questioning to you, I will refer to the Association of Emigrant Serbs as "the association," and my first question to you is where precisely did the association have its offices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The offices of the association were in Nusiceva Street, number 4, Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you to describe for the Chamber any prominent visitors that came to the office during the time that you were at the office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Various politicians would come. The leaders from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and from Republika Srpska would also come, as would members of the government of Serbia and people from the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to be a bit more specific. With respect to political leaders, can you describe the party or parties that those leaders belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mostly they belonged to the SPS and to the democratic party of Karadzic, the Serbian Democratic Party led by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you have described leaders from the Republic of Serb Krajina and from Republika Srpska. Can I ask you to identify the names of individuals from both of those entities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can say that from the Republika Srpska, Goran Hadzic would come often, and from Republika Srpska, various politicians. Whenever there were meetings, I could not attend nor could the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the names of any of the other people who came from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can. Krajisnik would come frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I once met with Biljana Plavsic in the government of Serbia, and then I drove her to the airport at Batajnica. She would come too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've identified members of the Serbian MUP as also visiting the office. Are you able to identify any particular names of people from that organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Isidor. He would set up the equipment for communications, radio equipment for communication with Krajina. Above the offices there was a centre for monitoring developments in Republika Srpska and in the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You are describing a person from the Serbian MUP setting up communications equipment. Do you know where those lines -- where the other end of those lines were located specifically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: What do you mean the other end? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You said that these lines were set up to monitor events in the Serbian Krajina, I believe. What I'm asking you is do you know in what particular location the other end of those communication lines were terminated, a particular organisation or a particular place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: There were radio communications, and the antennas were placed on the roof, and there were connections with various commands in the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the period of which you have knowledge, were there ever any members of the JNA or the VJ visiting the association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: As far as I know, a security officer came who worked in Korenica, but I cannot recollect his name, from the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the time that you're familiar with, was there ever anybody from the Serbian Ministry of Defence who visited the association's offices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: From the Defence Ministry, no one came. From the army, as far as I know, they didn't come to the association itself. Brana went to meetings, but they didn't come to the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe what you know about meetings with members of the association and members of the Ministry of Defence. How frequently, and where were those meetings held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: They were held on a daily basis. Every morning, there would be meetings in the state security of the MUP of Serbia where they would review information from the battlefront. And then Milan Prodanic would go to Bubanj Potok where he held meetings every afternoon with Boro Stanisic as to what should be sent where, to what part of the battlefront.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I leave this topic of the association's offices, were there ever any members of paramilitary organisations that you saw visit the office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. From Novi Sad, Lajnovic Dugi came, who later was killed. I remember him well coming there. Captain Dragan would also come.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can't remember. Kojic from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a time that Mr. Crncevic informed you about some special lines or telephone lines that he had installed in his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It's not a matter that he told me about; I saw those telephone lines. There were special telephone lines with Mr. Milosevic and the state security of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are special telephones, so-called red telephones, not ordinary telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, the people doing the translation are asking if you can speak a little bit louder. They're having difficulty hearing everything that you say. Could I ask you, the line that was connected to the -- I believe you said the Serbian state security or the MUP of Serbia, can you tell us, do you know who it was, whose office, that line was connected to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: At the other end of the line was the state security of MUP Serbia and Mr. Milosevic. The line was directly connected to them. Brana Crncevic had direct communication with them, not using regular lines but those special telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mr. Crncevic ever tell you what the purpose of having those direct lines was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The purpose of the direct lines was to know exactly what was happening on the theatre of war. Many people came to Brana Crncevic's offices to inform him about developments on the front and then he would convey that information to the state security and the former president, Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you detailed questions about the activities of the association, can I ask you, in summary fashion, to describe for the Chamber the portion of assistance that was rendered that you, I think believe -- I think you referred to it as "battlefield supplies." Can you give the Chamber some sense of what quantity of battlefield supplies or military equipment passed through the -- passed through the association to the battlefields of Bosnia and the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can say the exact number from Bubanj Potok in the 1992 -- in 1992 towards the end of the year. I think that more than 1.200 trucks of weapons and ammunition passed through Bubanj Potok, and transports by matica -- by the association participated. Then there were also vehicles of the MUP of Serbia that were engaged, as well as private transporters, and trucks were coming from Serbian Krajina and from Republika Srpska. And there was more than 1.200 heavyweight trucks. Not small ones of four and a half tons but those with more than 20 tons carrying capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the military equipment that was distributed by the association, do you know from where it came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: A part of it were radio stations, and these radio stations were received by the association from Serbian societies all over Europe and the world. Actually, the military equipment, the weapons and ammunition, they came from Bubanj Potok 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please be more precise about what was at Bubanj Potok. What type of facility? Who owned it? What type of facility was at Bubanj Potok from which the association received weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Bubanj Potok number 2 is one of the largest warehouses of ammunition and weapons in the former Yugoslavia. It supplied -- it provided weapons. These are large underground depots. There are hangars above ground. In addition to those depots, there is Bubanj Potok 1, which was used as a training ground and shooting range, and it is from there that people were sent to the front, and the two facilities about -- are about 2 kilometres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Bubanj Potok 2 where the ammunition and weapons were stored, who owned that facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The warehouse was owned by military post 5055, that is the command of the city of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if you know, was the relationship between the MUP of Serbia and either Bubanj Potok 1, the training facility, or Bubanj Potok 2, the storage facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The relationship between the MUP of Serbia and the warehouses was such there were only two men involved, Bora Stanisic and Milan Prodanic. Milan Prodanic came with the orders what should be carried and Bora Stanisic prepared the transport convoys and sent them off to the front. So the link with the state security of MUP in the MUP of Serbia was that a very small circle of people in the former JNA actually knew what was going on in Bubanj Potok, at least as far as I know. The same applies to the MUP of Serbia. A very small circle of people were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What percentage of the weapons and ammunition that were distributed by the association came from Bubanj Potok 2, from VP 5055?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: A very large per cent. It's not negligible. Nowadays, you could supply, well, one-third of the former Yugoslavia, say, as regards manpower. The figure speaks in itself. One thousand two hundred trucks in 1992. These are heavy trucks. You could arm a great many men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to simply list the names of any people who significantly contributed to the distribution of weapons from Bubanj Potok. You've mentioned Bora Stanisic already. Are there any other officers, either military or civilian employees, whose names should be recorded here as being involved in this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Bubanj Potok had a total of five persons. There was Dule Malusic. He was a sergeant in the military police. Then there was also a man called Rile. He was a civilian military person employed by the army of Yugoslavia. Then there was a man called Brka, and then there was a man called Buca who died. He was actually the main person in charge of warehouses in Bubanj Potok and he died during the war, but how he died is something that has never been explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there any particular piece of military equipment or weaponry that had to be purchased separately from what was received from these military warehouses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. The former JNA did not have silencers only, because this was not part of regular requirements. This was manufactured in Kaludjerica near Belgrade; a privately owned workshop manufactured them. The payments for these silencers were made, as far as I know, by the state security of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if you could clarify a couple of things with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First, whether Bubanj Potok is the name of a military facility or a name of a place. Secondly, whether it is in Belgrade or near Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, if I may clarify those points that Judge Kwon is inquiring about. Let's take Bubanj Potok. The place that you're referring to as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bubanj Potok 1, was that the official name or simply the name of the place where it was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is a locality. This is where the place actually was. It's outside Belgrade, a few kilometres on the road to Nis. You get off the highway, after a few kilometres Bubanj Potok 1 is on the left-hand side. Bubanj Potok 2 is on the right-hand side. But the two facilities are divided. Both belonged to the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, Bubanj Potok 1, did it have any official name, let's say, at the gate or any official address that you can recall now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Quite simply, it was called Bubanj Potok 1. When you received call-up papers for mobilisation, it would say Bubanj Potok 1. That's where you were mobilised to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does the same hold true for Bubanj Potok 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. Bubanj Potok 2 was a closed facility. It only consisted of storage facilities for military equipment, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the weapons that -- and ammunition that the association received from Bubanj Potok 2, did it have a place where the association itself would temporarily store those weapons prior to them being distributed in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: In some cases, yes. We had some parking space at the Belgrade fairgrounds or, rather, the entrance to the Belgrade fairgrounds on the right-hand side. This is where some old workshops existed before. And then we were given this parking space so that vehicles could be parked there before they went to Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. For a while while Kertes was in the MUP, we had -- we had their hangars too in Makis, and that also belonged to the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, an earlier witness has talked about a location that he described as an overpass in the vicinity of the fairgrounds. Are you familiar with an overpass, an elevated highway, in the vicinity of the fairgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is right underneath the overpass. It's underneath the highway, the loop of highway is called the Gazelle. It's on the left-hand side. It's at the very entrance into the Belgrade fairgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the location you're describing as where the trucks would be parked, this is under a highway. Is that what you're describing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can put it that way, although it's a bit to the left compared to the highway, because there was this big haul of the Belgrade fairgrounds that the matica used for humanitarian aid, medicine and things like that, and that was right underneath the highway loop, and I don't know whether that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this storage facility, were -- did the association ever transport weapons directly from facilities belonging to the Serbian MUP, and if so, can you please identify the location of those facilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can identify them. There was a warehouse in Ostruznica that belonged to the MUP of Serbia, and that is where transports directly started as well. Later on, a warehouse was made towards the very end in Lipovica. The army of Yugoslavia gave this to the MUP of Serbia. This is E on the road leading to Barajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I am now going to ask that you be shown Exhibit 539, tab 2. It is a document dated the 1st of September, 1992. Can I ask you to look at it and tell us whether you recognise the document; and if so, please comment on its contents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the association got, 10.000 litres of diesel fuel for meeting its own needs, and it was by way of coupons for the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This fuel that the association received, was it used in the distribution of -- solely for the distribution of humanitarian aid, as indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. No. All this fuel was obtained for military and civilian aid. Also, we used fuel from military storage facilities. Bubanj Potok 2 had a gasoline station of their own, and we got fuel from there. And no payments were made for that fuel; we simply received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 539, tab 3, and I'd ask you the same question, sir: If you can identify this document; and if so, please describe its -- its meaning to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is a document of the Ministry for Communications with Serbs outside Serbia. The address is Nusiceva number 4, and this gives approval to take over 2.500 litres of fuel in accordance with the decision of the ministry of the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now ask you to take a look at Exhibit 539, tab 4. It is an undated piece of paper containing a list of numbers. Can I ask you to describe what is the significance of the names and phone numbers contained on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: These are telephone numbers of Jugopetrol, Beopetrol, and the Nafta gas company from Novi Sad. There were contacts with them when certain amounts of fuel were required. These are the direct telephone numbers of the general managers of Jugopetrol, Dragan Tomic; the director of the former Beopetrol, Mileta Nedjo; and contacts were made with him, if necessary, to take over fuel from their storage facilities or gasoline stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, so that the record is clear, I've just been asking you questions about military equipment and ammunition. Would it be fair to say that significant amounts of humanitarian - purely humanitarian - aid were also distributed by the association to those people in need in both the battle-torn areas of Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to take a look at tab 5 of Exhibit 539, and my question to you is in this document dated the 19th of June, 1992, is this not a record of one such shipment of purely humanitarian aid going to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This aid was sent to Sarajevo. The government of the Republic of Serbia was sending humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. These are different amounts of sugar, flour, oil, everything else that was sent to the area of Pale and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now ask you to take a look at tab 6 of 539. Can you please identify this document - it's a document dated the 17th of June, 1992 - and describe its contents for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is a document of the Red Cross of Serbia to the government of the Republic of Serbia, to the Ministry for Communication with Serbs Outside Serbia. This is a document requesting that humanitarian aid be brought to the Red Cross warehouses from where matica trucks were supposed to transport it to Pale and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you involved in one such convoy that transported humanitarian aid from Belgrade to Pale near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the course of that convoy or your duties to deliver that convoy, did you have a meeting with Mr. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. In that particular case, I actually met with Radovan Karadzic in Pale. Biljana Plavsic and Radovan Karadzic. I had some problems precisely with Radovan Karadzic, because he would not allow me to take a number of trucks that were intended for Sarajevo to Sarajevo itself. He asked for all the trucks to be unloaded in Pale. I opposed that. I would not allow all the trucks to be unloaded in Pale because it was written on the trucks themselves by the Red Cross people that this aid was sent to Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. Actually, to Merhamet and Caritas, the charity organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now ask you to look at Exhibit 539, tab 8. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document too. This is a document that was received by the Association of Serbs from the public security station in Donji Lapac in Lika, specifying all the equipment they needed for this police station of theirs in Donji Lapac. Most of this is military materiel. Among this materiel, inter alia, silencers were being requested for automatic rifles; 35 for sniper rifles, for 7.9-millimetre rifles, and for Scorpios silencers as well, 15 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this document, is this document an example of the types of documents that would be sent to the association requesting ammunition and military equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified earlier about Mr. Prodanic and Bora Stanisic having meetings. Can I ask you to describe where they would have those meetings and with what frequency.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The meetings between Milan Prodanic and Bora Stanisic at first took place at the warehouse of Bubanj Potok 2. There was a small office within the hall itself. It's a makeshift office, a very small one. It was made mostly for the winter, because these hangars are very cold during the winter. However, these conversations could be overheard as well because it wasn't a properly built room. Later on, these meetings were held at the matica hall every afternoon at the Belgrade fairgrounds. That's where humanitarian aid was kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've testified that the meetings that were held at Bubanj Potok 2 could be overheard. Did you yourself ever overhear those conversations; and if so, could I ask you to just briefly summarise the types of subjects that were discussed at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, at these meetings supplies with ammunition and weapons in parts and Bosnia and Croatia, that's what was discussed; what was necessary, what amounts, what kind of weapons, what kind of ammunition. For the most part, that is what these meetings dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You testified earlier about other meetings that were held at the state security building. Can I ask you to be more specific in telling us who would attend these meetings and with what frequency these meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, meetings at the state security took place every day or, rather, every morning. As far as I know, these meetings were held including the following people: Milan Prodanic, Jovica Stanisic, Tepavcevic, and for a while Mihalj Kertes while he was at the federal MUP. I don't know about the rest but as far as these people are concerned, I heard that they attended these meetings. Mr. Milosevic was also informed about these meetings every day, because I know that when they had discussions in my presence, Mr. Milosevic would have to be informed about these meetings every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber how it is you know about these meetings that were held every morning in the state security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, of course I know, because when additional amounts of weapons were requested, whenever Prodanic came to Bubanj Potok 2, he would say at the meeting we received information as to what was necessary in which part of the front line so that these deliveries could be made from Bubanj Potok itself. Because the MUP of Serbia itself did not have such large storage facilities and so many weapons in order to be able to send all of this to the front line. Actually, all the military equipment that came from the former Yugoslav republics, from Slovenia, from Croatia, from Macedonia, for the most part was brought to the Bubanj Potok storage facilities and the other storage facilities around Belgrade. So for such weapons -- so as far as these weapons were concerned, they didn't have to be accounted for. There would always be a certain amount that could remain within the storage facility of Bubanj Potok 2 and thus be accounted for. And these weapons didn't have to be recorded, the other ones. As for all these weapons that were needed, over a certain period of time the Territorial Defence of Serbia was abolished. These weapons of the Territorial Defence of Serbia were taken to the front line, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The front line where, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, all these places there where of course there were headquarters that received this equipment. At first all of them were civilians. These were not military personnel. It wasn't professional policemen or military personnel who were involved. These were ordinary citizens who were establishing the so-called Territorial Defence at the time, and this ammunition and these weapons were sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The meetings at the state security office of the Serbian MUP, did Mr. Crncevic ever go to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I think he went to these meetings only on a few occasions. He would come to work very late in general. He was a late sleeper in the morning, as far as I know. And the meetings were held early in the morning. Brana Crncevic went to see Jovica Stanisic, I know that. They were good friends. They even visited each other at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When he -- you say that he would go see or visit Jovica Stanisic. Was this a social visit or a business visit, and where precisely would he go see Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: To the MUP of Serbia. It is a purely business relationship. It's not a private relationship, personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait a second, please. Mr. B-179, you said that Mr. Milosevic must have been receiving the daily report from the meeting. Could you elaborate on how you came to know that a little more? You said that you had overheard something. What is it that exactly you heard from their conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard in Bubanj Potok conversations between Milan Prodanic and Jovica Stanisic, that the president, Mr. Milosevic at the time, had to be informed about everything that was being done. After all, Mr. Milosevic, although he did not command the army, the supreme defence command, it was the MUP of Serbia that was under his command and the state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your assumption that Mr. Milosevic received the daily report from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not my assumption. It's the truth. He received reports. I heard that he received reports from Milan Prodanic, from the state security of Serbia, from the head of the state security of Serbia. It's not an assumption. I heard this with my very own ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could you tell me what you heard at that time exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I mean on various occasions, I heard that Mr. Milosevic had to be informed about everything that was being sent to the front line. The meetings themselves were held at the state security of the MUP of Serbia in this small circle of people. Milan Prodanic came from these meetings to Bubanj Potok, and he directly conveyed this to Mr. Jovica Stanisic and to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome, apart from that, I think you haven't dealt with the paragraph 19 in the summary and the following paragraphs. Was it your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you for pointing that out. I'll return to that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I return to questions that I inadvertently omitted, when you would hear Mr. Prodanic refer to conversations with Mr. Milosevic, what term did he use sometimes to refer to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: They called him "Dad." They would say, "That is what Dad ordered."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, prior to the association receiving weapons and ammunition from Bubanj Potok 2 and distributing it, would -- who would have to give permission for those weapons to be released from Bubanj Potok 2 and given to the association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You mean permission in terms of having the weapons handed over to the matica so that they could then be transported further to the front line? Is that what you mean? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, I should put it this way: In order to load the weapons onto the trucks, it was Lieutenant Colonel Bora Stanisic from Bubanj Potok who gave orders to that effect. Then it was sent to Bubanj Potok, and then weapons and ammunition were boarded on those trucks. If necessary, medicine and blankets and food were added on to the trucks in the hall of the matica, and then from there the trucks went to different frontlines. It was the MUP of Serbia that issued orders concerning this, and I can explain in which way, so that -- I mean, we did not need any special permission for these transports in order to cross checkpoints of the Ministry of the Interior. Policemen were always informed that such-and-such vehicles would be passing there, and nobody checked these vehicles in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who would Lieutenant Colonel Bora Stanisic receive his orders from? Would it be his military superior or someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. No way. It would not be his military superior. It would be the MUP of Serbia; Milan Prodanic specifically and directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, what is your understanding about how orders to distribute weapons belonging to the JNA and VJ, what would have been the regular course of that order to give out such weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, it should have been going through the Ministry of Defence and the army of Yugoslavia. However, it didn't go through the Ministry of Defence of Yugoslavia or the army. That would have been the proper course. However, this proper course was bypassed in this case. This work was not supposed to be known about by a great number of people. Only a small number of people knew about it in the circle that I dealt in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can change the subject and ask you: Were you personally involved in some convoys that distributed weapons to the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, a number of times. I went twice to Zvecevo. I was on convoys led by Bora Stanisic. Sometimes -- for a while, in fact, these convoys started from Bubanj Potok every Friday, would come back on Saturday. Those were pretty large convoys. I usually went to a hospital in Bucje, near Zvecevo, where I dropped off medicine, blankets and other aid, but sometimes I went all the way to Zvecevo where military equipment was stored for that part of the battlefield, the front line. Also, there was one convoy that I led myself instead of Bora Stanisic. It included four trucks that carried ammunition for Podnoble [phoen] at the time of battles in Slavonski Brod and Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the first time you were involved in one of these convoys. Can I ask you to describe how many trucks in total were involved in the convoy, and can you give us some idea about which percentage of those trucks were carrying humanitarian aid and which were carrying military equipment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You mean for Zvecevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, usually there would be ten to 15 trucks. One truck would be carrying only humanitarian aid and other trucks would carry military assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in a convoy in which the Serbian state security had provided the trucks to transport the material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Certainly. In most of these convoys, the trucks of the MUP of Serbia were involved. It is true that their trucks were slightly smaller. Those were Mercedes trucks, Mercedes 12 and 13. Their carrying capacity was slightly lower, but they were usually used for carrying supplies within the convoys. Also, there was a time when the MUP of Serbia had a Renault trailer truck that was brought from the front line as war booty. And I know that they were not able to start it for a while because this cab of the truck was operated by remote control.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I can draw your attention to the Republika Srpska, that part of Bosnia. Are you aware of convoys, similar convoys being sent into areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. They sent supplies to all parts of Bosnia, from Sarajevo all the way up to Herzegovina. There were liaison persons, contact persons designated by the MUP of Serbia. They were mainly civilians. As for Sarajevo itself, the liaison was a woman nicknamed Beba, who before the war used to own a cafe in Sarajevo, in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you just to simply list the different locations in Bosnia that you have personal knowledge that convoys of weapons were sent to these locations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, supplies were sent to Knin, Gracac, Licka Osijek, also Banja Luka, to Nevesinje in Herzegovina, to Trebinje, although these are very remote places looking from Belgrade, but Belgrade supplied that part of the front line as well. Maybe there were other sources of supplies, but I didn't know about that other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with what frequency did these convoys go into Bosnia? Can you give us a -- was it every week, every month? Can you give us some idea of the frequency with which they travelled to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, convoys went practically on a daily basis. They came and went from Bubanj Potok practically every day. They would come back from the front line, from Croatia and Bosnia, and then they would -- these trucks coming from these areas would load supplies and drive it back to their own locations. Trucks came and went every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the convoys that went to Bosnia, did they go before the conflict broke out, after the conflict broke out, or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Before the conflict, one truck -- I mean, before the conflict in Bosnia, one Scania truck from the association took from Bubanj Potok weaponry to Sarajevo before the conflict broke out in Sarajevo. It was a Scania truck driven by Zeljko Rajcevic who is a professional driver of the association, a refugee from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to describe what was the arrangement with the people who would receive these weapons? Would they have to pay for these weapons? What would happen when the weapons were delivered to the locations in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. This weaponry was not paid for. It was just received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the people receiving the weapons have to sign that they had received them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody had to sign a receipt issued by the command of the city of Belgrade, military post box 5055, and it accompanied on a compulsory basis every truck that was sent out. All these receipts had to be signed for the entire amount contained in the truck, ammunition and weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 539, tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you, can you identify this document, how it is you identify this document, and describe its contents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is one of the receipts of the military post 5055, the Belgrade city defence command. It concerned 82-millimetre shells for mortars. The quantity indicated is 225, and that fitted into one van. I personally took it over from Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that your -- is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature, meaning that I received it and delivered it to the man who was designated to me from Gabos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this document has at the top of it for the following materiel received for temporary use. A number of the documents seem to refer that some of this equipment was loaned rather than given outright. My question to you is: Were you ever involved or ever aware of similar transportation carrying back weapons and ammunition from the places from where it was distributed to -- from the places it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. By no means I never returned these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there ever an occasion when you were making a delivery or involved in a delivery when Arkan and his men sought to join the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. It was our first travel to Knin, first journey. The first convoy, when it was very difficult to reach Knin and Banja Luka. It was the first convoy that set out for Knin, included me. There was a meeting at a petrol station where I was supposed to meet up with the rest of the convoy that did not belong to my organisation. I had behind me my part of the personnel in my vehicles, and when I came to this petrol station outside of Belgrade, I was met by the vehicles and the men belonging to Arkan. When I realised that those were Arkan's men, knowing what they were doing and what they were dealing with, I ordered my men to start their trucks and to return to the depots where we had started from. However, after awhile, Arkan came with 10 to 15 of his men who were pointing his guns, his automatic rifles, at me and my men. He slapped me, and he told me to order my trucks to start and drive on. In order not to risk the lives of my men, I had to do as he said. Arkan accompanied that convoy up to Modrica, and then he probably returned to new Belgrade; whereas I continued my journey across Plitvice all the way to Knin and only --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, that's sufficient detail with Mr. Arkan's involvement in the convoy. You mentioned the association transporting radio transmitters. I just want to ask that you be shown tab 7 of 539. Without going into too much detail, is this document a receipt for a quantity of radio transmitters given to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This is a receipt referring to radio transmitters that I gave to Biljana Plavsic for the headquarters of Republika Srpska, and it is directly related, intended for Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Plavsic sign that receipt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when General Mladic asked to see some of the people involved in the supply of the VRS with weapons? Again, the detail of the conversation is not as important as just telling us when and where it was you met General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, I was at Bubanj Potok 2 when we received a telephone call when it was said that General Mladic wanted to see us, to see who was supplying him with weapons, who was doing that part of the work, and he was waiting for us in a coffee bar near the new Belgrade municipality building, and that was the first time I saw General Mladic in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there an occasion when you were asked to escort a truckload of Republic of Serb Krajina dinars from Belgrade to Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. I was told to send a truckload, and it was again a Scania truck, which is a closed truck, not with a tarpaulin but it had a completely closed box. They told me to load it with money. Those were the first Krajina dinars printed at the mint in Topcider. It was driven again by this man Jovo, who was a refugee from Western Slavonia. He went to the mint and took over between seven and eight tons of banknotes that we sent to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Also, we carried back from Knin a certain amount of money of all currencies - German marks, dollars, et cetera - and they were driven to the mint at Topcider. That was on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified about being able to pass through checkpoints without any difficulty. I'd ask that you be shown tab 9 of 539 and ask you, are you able to identify this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document. It concerns a bus with Vukovar licence plates, which I drove myself. I have a licence for driving trucks, and I was driving refugees to Lazarevac to a centre for accommodation of refugees, and these used to be barracks for accommodation of miners from that area. The very name of Brana Crncevic made it very easy for us to make our passage anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Whose responsibility was it to notify border crossings and checkpoints, to arrange for the unimpeded access of the trucks transporting weapons for the association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: That was done by Milan Prodanic, head of the 6th administration of the state security of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the embargo against the Republika Srpska, was there any significant change in the level of supplies that went from the association to areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, there was no particular change. It continued, but the vehicles had to be removed from Bubanj Potok. They couldn't stay on long. One or two trucks at most would come in at a time, and then they had to be removed after being loaded so as to prevent leakage of the information that this loading was being done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified earlier about being aware of meetings held in the state security and also of Mr. Milosevic being notified or wanting to be kept informed about the transportation of these weapons. Are you able to say that during the embargo these meetings continued or are you not able to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Meetings were held even during the embargo. At that time, the meetings were held on the premises of the association, namely, this hall at the Belgrade fairgrounds that belonged to the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness now be shown Exhibit 539, tab 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, sir, if you're able to identify this document, and if so, please describe its contents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: This is one of the applications by Brana Crncevic to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia in Nemanjina Street, that is, the government building of Serbia, applying for 15 automatic rifles, eight pistols, four automatic Skorpio pistols, and 500 9-millimetre rounds for pistols. This was approved, and it says here precisely that this was settled and that Boro should give it to the association. In fact, he gave it directly to me, and I distributed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask now that the witness be shown 539, tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is a series of documents. The specific detail of the documents isn't as important as whether or not you're able to identify what they are; and if you are, can you summarise the general nature of these various documents.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: These are again the documents of military post 5055 concerning the weapons and ammunition that I took over on behalf of the Association of Serbs and Serbian Expatriots.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the equipment described in those documents in tab 11, would it be fair to say that that equipment was ultimately then redistributed by the association to places in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. These weapons and ammunitions were directly meant for the association. It didn't go to Bosnia or Croatia. It was given to people who worked for the association and for practice purposes, because our staff, our people, were taken to target practice because they had to undergo training.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So these documents represent equipment directly issued to the association for the purpose of its distribution, not for actual distribution to a third party itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a time when the association was requested to transport actual paramilitary members, members of paramilitary units, to areas in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. On a couple of occasions, Brana was asked to secure trucks for members of various formations that were sent from Bubanj Potok 1. Brana was one of the few people who had enough authority for his requests to be met whenever he asked transport companies like Lasta or any others for trucks of their own to be given to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Finally, I'd ask that the witness be shown tab 13 of 539.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And once again, sir, I'd ask you if you can recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This is a thank you note addressed to me from the army of Yugoslavia for my commitment and self-effacing efforts in lending assistance to members of the Territorial Defence and the Serbian people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who were exposed to Ustasha terror and genocide. This was issued by military post 5055, it was signed by Colonel Radoslav Blazic, but honestly I don't even know who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I have no further questions for you. I would remind you that when you're being asked questions by Mr. Milosevic, that you keep an eye on the red light on his microphone and only begin your answer after that light has been turned off. And if I could advise the Chamber, the only particular areas of sensitivity the Prosecution ask be taken in private session would be the specific job description and title of this witness in the association as well as any other questioning about the previous court proceedings which are listed on page 14 of the summary. Other than that, it is the Prosecution's position that none of it will compromise the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registry raised the question of which matters should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could identify those at this stage. They would be tab 1, tab 3, tab 4, tab 9, tab 11, tab 12, and tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take the usual adjournment now. It will be for 20 minutes. Witness B-179, could you be back in 20 minutes, please, to go on with your evidence. Could you remember this: During the course of those adjournments, don't speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we've decided you should have one hour and a half for cross-examination of this witness. That should be ample time provided you don't argue with him and waste time with other peripheral issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I won't waste time on peripheral issues, Mr. May, though this witness is telling untruths from beginning to end, and therefore, I will have to examine him in some detail, so I'm not sure that I will be able to fit my cross-examination with your envisaged hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can deal with your first suggestion. Witness B-179, you've heard what the accused has alleged. He's alleged that you've been telling untruths from beginning to end. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he is a liar, I am not. I do not lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. B-179, I see you gave this statement to the investigators on the 11th and 12th of March, 2003. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the motive for giving this statement to the investigators is to show that Serbs are not a genocidal people. You say, "My motivation for contacting and deliver these documents are to show that the population of Serbia are not the genocide type of people." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is in your statement. Do you have your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, I don't, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what does this word "genocide" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Genocide is killing of one people, Mr. Milosevic. You, as the President of Serbia, inflicted the greatest damage and genocide to your own people, the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at your statement, Mr. B-179, and to mark on it the places, paragraphs, or sentences in which you acted in accordance with this motive, that is, your motivation, as you say, to show that Serbs are not genocidal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examination is not a form of trick or anything like that or any sort of test for the witness. Now, if you want to ask the witness questions, you can, but he cannot possibly comply with that suggestion. Now, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question, Mr. May, was to ask the witness to point to parts of his statement which corroborate what he says he's doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I heard that, and I've told you that you cannot ask that question. It's not a test for the witness. It's not a proper question, or a trick which you seem to be playing. Now, you can rephrase your question if you want to ask it, or you must move on to a new one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'll move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you say that for you there is no written trace that you ever took part in any kind of war operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I'll answer that question. According to the war assignment, I come under the military post 5055. Nowhere in my military booklet is it indicated that during the war I took part in the work of any unit of the VP 5055. Also, you know very well that all the documents for Bubanj Potok were burnt. I heard with my own ears when it was stated, that is a conversation between Bora Stanisic and Milan Prodanic who said that all those documents had been destroyed by fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean there were minutes of those conversations between Stanisic and Prodanic and then they were burnt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. Minutes were not kept of their conversations, but the documents of VP 5055 that were sent to the front accompanying weapons and ammunition, those documents that went with the transports were burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. B-179, you point out also that on many occasions you risked your own life for the convoys to reach places that were under siege; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who could have killed you, as you say that you were risking your life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Who could kill me? Among others, they could have killed me in Western Slavonia. Whenever we went to Zvecevo in a convoy, fire was opened at us from artillery weapons. Also, there were quite a lot of tricks when I was driving the truck to Sarajevo on the way there and back. If you remember the first convoy of the government of Serbia sent to Pale, Cvijan was on television announcing that a convoy of aid was leaving for Pale that morning. I didn't go early, as planned intentionally, but I left at noon, and instead of my column, another column was framed. Eleven drivers were killed from Milici who were transporting ore. I was told that the road to Milici from Zvornik was safe. I went around a different way. Instead of via Milici, I went via Sekovici to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, you say that you risked your life to reach the places that were under siege; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who held those places under siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: If you mean -- I can give you the example of Mirkovci. On one occasion, I was tasked to drive Dr. Aco Todorovic from the Emergency Ward and two technicians, only one arrived. However, when I reached Sid, the driver who was to take them over with other medical equipment didn't dare go. He was elderly man, and he was frightened, and he didn't dare go to Mirkovci. That time, I asked the president of the municipality, Ljilja Popovic, as no one wanted to go with them, I continued with them to Mirkovci, and I passed through various barricades. I also crossed the Sarajevo airfield amid shooting, but my people didn't kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But who held those places under siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this means that Serbs in Croatia in many places were besieged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs attack the Croats and place themselves under siege or were they attacked and that is how they came to be under siege?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, one could give you a very lengthy answer to that question. I've seen so much that I don't know whom to trust any more. I'll give you an example from those very Mirkovci. On that journey to Mirkovci, I was escorted by two tanks, a van that I drove, and another truck that was transporting weapons. Look at this absurdity of yours. In that truck there were weapons for Mirkovci. It was distributed to the citizens of Mirkovci. And in Mirkovci, you had one of the major warehouses of weapons and ammunitions. I think you are very familiar with this location, Vrapcana. I had a lot of trouble with offices of the state security of the army of Yugoslavia because of that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know anything about Vrapcana and storage of weapons there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You will understand, because from Vrapcana it was the Croatian army that was supplied with weapons and ammunition. An officer, a JNA officer, a captain would transport weapons to Vinkovci every morning in four trucks. In those days, he was the commander. The commander in Mirkovci was Belgan [phoen]. We asked those trucks to be searched one day and the captain would not allow it. And it is common knowledge when trucks leave what they look like when they're full. You can see how heavy they are when they weigh down on the wheels, and you can see what they look like when they're empty. So you were arming both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We were arming both sides, were we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Not we, but you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, B-179. I hear that assertion for the first time. Now, tell me, please, as you say in paragraph 2 of your statement, you were a member of the Serbian Renewal Movement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I was never a member of any party, of the League of Communists or any of your parties, but I joined the Serbian Renewal Movement precisely to topple your regime in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as a member of that party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, SPO, you must know that the SPO headed all the opposition activities directed against what you call the regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Let me tell you something, Vozdovac municipality, where I reside, the SPO was in power and the SPS and JUL. So you can't say that the opposition was in power. You were in power. I felt the consequences very well on my own back. Your authorities first tried to seize my house, then to destroy my --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not talk about your house and who wanted to seize your house, et cetera. I really wouldn't like to go into such things here now. As a volunteer during 1991, 1992, 1993, that is the period you're testifying about, you worked as a volunteer in the Association of Emigrants; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. I was a volunteer in that association. When aid was asked for Borovo Selo, Brano Crncevic announced over the media an appeal for help to Borovo Selo and to assist the refugees crossing the Sava River. I had a large boat that I made myself with two engines, Yamaha and Mercury, and I made a gift them to Borovo Selo and went there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many volunteers in the course of 1991, 1992, and 1993 were sent by the SPO to the front in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. I had no interest in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember when Vuk Draskovic founded the so-called Serbian Guards? I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I know something about it. I think there were offices also in Nusiceva Street. That is Vuk Draskovic's offices, close to the matica, in fact. As I say, I was never involved in politics. It never interested me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Vuk Draskovic in those days was a politician who said that every hand that isn't a Serbian hand should be cut off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't remember that statement of his? Was that a call for conflict and war or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't remember the statement, so there's not much point asking him that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just to establish the real motives for your testimony, in addition to testifying here, as you yourself said, you are my political opponent. That's how you described yourself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, when you came to power, to be quite sincere, I thought an intelligent man had come to lead the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my questions briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Why briefly? I have to give you a full answer. I can't give you a yes or no answer. But with subsequent developments, I drew my own conclusions and an opinion about you, and formed an opinion about you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you came to the Emigrants Association upon your own initiative, disturbed by the fact -- by the well-known event when Mr. Seskocevic [phoen] drowned, a man from Borovo Selo, because his boat capsized? And you contributed to the humanitarian fund for refugees from Croatia your own boat, you offered your own boat to transport people from Borovo Selo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. I gave them a metal boat that I made myself. It was for 12 men. A bullet couldn't pierce it because it was made of steel sheeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you volunteered to transport refugees from Croatia and humanitarian aid through the only then established refugee camps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was assumed at the time that, as a patriot, you wanted to help the humanitarian activities of the matica, of the association; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: The humanitarian aid to the whole people, not just the matica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the humanitarian activities of the matica, of the association, which was distributing aid all over. That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. No, it is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is it true from one humanitarian activity you didn't return? You stayed in Mirkovci of your own free will for a couple of months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to information I have, you stayed there for a couple of months, and you did arms trading over there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, it's not right, Mr. Milosevic. I entered Mirkovci nine times and left Mirkovci. Now, what kind of weapons could I trade in? Where would I get the weapons from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You enumerated enormous quantities of weapons that you allegedly transported.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's why I'm saying you had them if you claim that you were transporting them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I think I said a moment ago that I went to Mirkovci accompanied by a truck with weapons that was distributed in Mirkovci. I didn't say that I was transporting those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. B-179. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that this be redacted and any remaining questions about the specific position this witness held be taken in closed session or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any more questions on this topic, Mr. Milosevic? If so, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. B-179, that convoys were organised occasionally when humanitarian aid had been gathered from various quarters, including from Serbs in the diaspora, and for the drivers, volunteers were chosen, and it could be a representative of the company who had collected the most food or sanitary material or even Serbs from the diaspora who were willing to go with that convoy of aid organised by the Emigrants Association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, that's not true. All -- I led all the transports with my men who were armed. No one else could have taken those transports. I headed all those transports of humanitarian aid from the Serbs Association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Deal with the other point the accused makes. He alleges that convoys were organised occasionally when humanitarian aid had been gathered from various quarters. Is that an accurate description of what was happening or not? Yes. Could you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, you're asking me. Well, let me tell you, it was like this: I would take a humanitarian convoy from Vojvodina when the locals were sending aid for the Lika battlefront. It consisted of 18 trucks. Those were those occasional convoys. What affected me most in those convoys, let me tell you straight away, when I reached the final destination, Gracac, it was requested that things would be loaded onto other trucks and taken to shops, to outlets, instead of being distributed to the people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I move on, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, Mr. Groome asked you to mention all the places you went to, and I wrote down here what you said. You say that you went twice in convoys that went to Zvecevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's right. But you didn't get to Zvecevo itself. You stopped somewhere; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. I handed over my equipment at Bucje. That was equipment for a hospital, but I continued to Zvecevo with the rest of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you handed over what you had for Bucje, there was a hospital at Bucje wasn't it, Mr. 179?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you gave blankets and medicines and things of that sort to the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not bring any weapons to Bucje, you gave them medical equipment, blankets and other things that a hospital needs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Not me, but Bora Stanisic took the convoy further. I mentioned that. And the other part of the convoy that went to Zvecevo was ammunition and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you went twice in these convoys to Zvecevo. Once you went in a convoy to the region of Bosanski Brod; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I led that convoy. It was a purely military convoy. It wasn't humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. From what I see here, you say that you were in a convoy that went to Zvecevo -- rather, two for Zvecevo, one for Bosanski Brod and one that went to Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Inter alia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you lead any other convoy except for these four that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. I can list more if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Repeat the question, would you, please. We're having some trouble with the monitors here. I take it that the transcript is still running. I'm told that it is. Yes. Could you repeat the question, please, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding on the basis of what you said that you were in two convoys for Zvecevo, one convoy that went to the area of Bosanski Brod and one convoy that went to Sarajevo. That is what you mentioned in response to the questions put to you by Mr. Groome. Tell me now, what were these other convoys in addition to the four ones that you mentioned? What were the other ones that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I can mention others. You probably remember the number of people in Smoluca, between 4.000 and 7.000 of them that were surrounded for months. I also led the humanitarian convoy that went to Smoluca. Is that perhaps incorrect as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see you, and it's the first time I've heard of you. How can I say whether it was correct whether you led a convoy or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you claim that -- you claim that you held a position for which I claim, according to the information provided by the matica, never even existed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, officially for you none of us who were involved in this line of work existed.
