utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that this kind of position did existed and that you actually held that job?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That does not explain at all what I'm asking you right now. In tab 9, you provided an authorisation given by the Matica of Emigrants, and you can see that it was signed by Brana Crncevic, president of the matica, and it says here in tab 9 that this is an authorisation enabling a vehicle, a bus, TAM, registration plates such-and-such. It can be used on behalf of the Centre of Serbs and Emigrants of Serbia, Nusiceva 4 Belgrade, for the needs of refugees from Croatia. So you have this document where it says that you, as a bus driver, namely that this bus and that you as its driver have the job of meeting the needs and helping emigrants from Croatia, refugees from Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. That is only one of the authorisations given for transporting persons, refugees, actually, to the prefabricated buildings of the Lazarevac mine. And what you've been claiming, that I never had that job and that I never received payments for it, I have a document, and I would like you to see it. The matica paid me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute, you're giving evidence to a court, not a private conversation with him. Do you know anything about this, Mr. Groome? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure what document the witness is referring to now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got anybody who can help translate it here? I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would be able to have it translated within the hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll try and deal with this, Witness, by -- if you would hand it over to Mr. Groome, he can have a look at it and then we'll try and put it to the accused in a moment, but let's deal with it by starting with Mr. Groome. Yes. Mr. Milosevic, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As regards this document, as far as I managed to understand what you were saying a few minutes ago, this is a document that confirmed that they paid you your salary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, that's the information I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, look, if you're going to ask any more questions about the witness or his jobs, you must do so in private session. Now, you know those rules. Now, do you want to ask any more questions along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just want to clarify this, Mr. May, but let's wait then and take a look at this document and then I'll put questions in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no need for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go into private session, and then we'll see if we can go into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 179. You say that during the war, the matica distributed to the Serbs in Croatia some assistance and that 80 per cent were donations given by Serbs who lived abroad. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the kind of assistance I'm talking about, because that is what the matica dealt with, humanitarian aid. And then you say that the government of Serbia financed the matica. Do you know for how long the matica has been in existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I know that it's been in existence for a very long time. I don't know exactly how many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then I'm not going to ask you about that. And is it correct then, Mr. B-179, that Serbs, regardless of whether they were Serbs from the diaspora or Serbs from Serbia itself, used the matica, the association, to send humanitarian aid through it in various forms to Serbs in Bosnia and to Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. The matica was used for that. Who else? At any rate, all assistance coming from the diaspora went through the matica for the most part. After awhile the bureau of the Government of Republika Srpska was opened, and then part of this aid went through them. I can also tell you that there were two trucks that were used by the matica were actually given to this bureau of the Government of Republika Srpska so that they could use them for this aid. These were actually trailer trucks from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this, Mr. B-179. Matica did receive donations, financial donations, from citizens of Serbia, from emigrants, and used that money to buy food, medicine, and other things that they sent by way of humanitarian aid; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The matica decided how and in which way it would use the money it received by way of donations, and they used that money to send aid to those they thought were needy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this money was used as humanitarian aid only and no weapons were ever bought from that money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's correct. Weapons were never bought.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that humanitarian aid often came in the form of food, medicines, clothing, and other things that were needed and that were then again sent through the matica to the places where the population was in greatest peril?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: That is correct. There was a hall at Belgrade fairgrounds where all these things were accumulated and then sent further on by way of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This hall at the Belgrade fairgrounds where all the aid came to, this was primarily clothing, medicine, food, blankets; other things that were needed. There weren't any weapons there; isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, not really. Once I brought some 120-millimetre mortars to that hall from the warehouses, the military warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You brought mortars to the hall of the Matica of Emigrants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: From your testimony here and from the documents that you provided, I saw that you stated that the only exception was when a few radio transmitters were taken to some headquarters in Croatia and Bosnia, and you proved that by way of some document, and you say it was signed by Biljana Plavsic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's right. But there is another thing. You forgot that I also had parking space for trucks at the entrance into Belgrade fairgrounds, on the right-hand side. That is where the vehicles with ammunition and weapons were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not clear to me. Could you please explain this to me. Where did these vehicles with weapons and ammunition come from to the parking space of the matica? What were they doing in the parking space of the matica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Precisely because they were not supposed to spend any time in Bubanj Potok, they were not supposed to spend any time at the MUP warehouses. They had to be kept in innocent locations, if we are going to call them that. As a matter of fact, even at my own plot of land sometimes these trucks with ammunition and weapons were kept so that the public could not be aware of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You kept such trucks at your very own plot of land? Did somebody from the matica tell you that you should keep trucks with weapons and ammunition on your own plot of land?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Bora Stanisic and Milan Prodanic did. Don't tell me that Milan Prodanic was not acting on your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any -- as far as I know, Milan Prodanic is an official of the state security. Tell me now, this document that you provided here in relation to the radio transmitters and you say that it was signed by Biljana Plavsic, is this a document that you gave to the investigators or did the investigators give this document to you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. I gave this document to the investigators. I picked up Biljana Plavsic that time at the government of Serbia. I used my own car to take her to the airport in Batajnica where she boarded a helicopter, and that's where she signed this document for me that she received these radio transmitters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did these radio transmitters come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: They by JAT aircraft from Germany, Yugoslav Airlines aircraft from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now: You say that the president of the matica, Brana Crncevic -- was Brana Crncevic. He's a writer otherwise. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's a well-known writer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that he was a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you now, now, whether he was a member of the Socialist Party -- you answer my question: Was he at the congress of the Socialist Party of Serbia in Sava centre as an associate member of the Socialist Party of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Brana Crncevic was never a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia, and he could have been there as a guest at some event, including the congress itself, but he was never a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: He used to say that he was an associate member. I don't know what it means to be an associate member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He could not have said that he was an associate member because he was not a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is just a waste of time, this kind of discussion. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear to you that Brana Crncevic could have been only one of the many guests there? In no other capacity could he have been there because he was not a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. This is a point you know about, whether he was or not a member. The witness doesn't. So what is the point of wasting time like this on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have that document now returned to court if the -- I'm not sure -- I can summarise basically what it is. It is unclear to us at this stage its relevance, but it's basically a contract signed between the -- this witness and other person of a fund that seems to have some dealings with the association or the matica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's there if the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just remind me what the matica association is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's the Association of Serbian Emigres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's also known as the matica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think "matica" is translation of "association."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In Serbian, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A proper translation is being done now. I'm not sure it will be down within the next few minutes, but it should be down before the cross-examination concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may not matter for the moment. Is this a matter which should be dealt with in private session? We'll deal with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think it should be, Your Honour, yes, if the accused is going to ask questions about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us go into private session, and let the accused see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this document by way of which the fund of the Serbian Association Nikola Tesla from Zurich is sending some equipment cannot be evidence that the Association of Emigrants of Serbia used its own money to purchase that equipment. Would it be fair to say that all donations received by the Association of Emigrants of Serbia were used to buy humanitarian aid for those who were in the greatest need?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what we said. That is not in dispute. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Are you aware, since you are talking about Brana Crncevic, do you know that he was at that time deputy to the Assembly of Serbia but as an independent deputy, a non-party candidate? He was not a member of any party, including the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I know that he was an assemblyman, but whether he was independent or not, I don't know. I never was involved in politics. I was not interested, and I'm still not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that in relation with the activities you were involved in, that you know that the Association of Emigrants transported more than 1.200 trucks with ammunition, weapons, and humanitarian aid to Krajina and the territory of the Republika Srpska. Do you say that here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: What I said is this: Among other things, the Association of Emigrants was involved in the transport of these 1.200 trucks. MUP vehicles and civilian vehicles and vehicles that came from the battlefield were also involved, not only the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want us to clear up one thing here. The Association of Emigrants of Serbia dealt in humanitarian aid. It did not deal in nor did it own any weapons that it could have sent to anyone. Is that true, Mr. 179, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, then why would I or my men get these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that because that is the only specific matter related to weapons and the Association of Emigrants. That's tab 10, and I would like you to look at it. It's signed by Brana Crncevic. It's possible that such a document exists. "Please issue for the purposes of the Association of Serbs and Serbian Emigrants for escorts of convoys and security to issue the following things: 15 automatic rifles, 8 pistols, 4 automatic pistols, 500 rounds and appropriate ammunition." So 15 automatic rifles, 8 pistols, 4 automatic pistols, and 500 rounds. But it is specified very clearly for the purposes of escorting convoys and security. We are talking about the security of those convoys carrying humanitarian aid. Is that correct, Mr. 179?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. This is the only document that passed through regular procedure, through the ministry, and there are many other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And if the association disposed of large amounts of weapons, as you say, why would it need to apply for these small amounts of weaponry for its own security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It had to apply because these people had to have appropriate licenses for carrying these weapons. And in order to have these licenses, you had to prove to the Ministry of Defence that you had received these weapons. In the beginning, it was Boro Stanisic who signed these licenses, and later on I got blanks of these -- blank forms of these licenses and I issued them myself and distributed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of securing convoys. Let me read here in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. handwriting. "Boro, please issue them by numbers under receipt valid up to two months, after which they should be returned."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, but that was only pro forma. "Bora" is Bora Stanisic from Bubanj Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what's written here. He must have been somebody who was authorised to order the person in charge to issue those weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. That must have been somebody in the government, and who from the government signed it, I don't know. You are in a better position to know than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it then clear from these documents that you produce here that the only weaponry applied for by the Association of Emigrants is the weaponry needed by men who were securing its convoys, because the convoys were travelling on unsafe roads through Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and needed security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. This assumption of yours is correct. The association did have a humanitarian line of work, but it had another line of work as well which you keep avoiding. Why don't you ask me a question about that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have information here that Brana Crncevic had never any contact whatsoever with any military post, including this military post 5055, in his capacity as president of the Association of Emigrants. He had nothing to do with it. As far as I can see, he didn't even address this military post for this weaponry for securing convoys. He wrote to the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer these assertions. Yes, Witness B-179.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. Milosevic, you claim one thing and I claim another. Brana Crncevic was a very good friend of both you and Jovica Stanisic, and as far as I know, you met very frequently. For you to deny something that I know about is not really possible. I even met up once with Jovica Stanisic when Boro got his rank of colonel. He was involved in the same line of work involving weapons and ammunition, and Crncevic was there and Jovica Stanisic and Milan Prodanic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is that supposed to confirm? Do you mean that it confirms that Brana Crncevic maintained special relations with that military post 5055?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Not the military post 5055 but with the MUP of Serbia, the state security department, and with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a good friend of Jovica Stanisic, and he's a good friend of mine - Brana Crncevic, I mean - but that has nothing to do with what we're talking about here. You even go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You don't dispute that he was a friend of yours, Crncevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is well known, Mr. May. Brana Crncevic is a well-known writer, president of the Emigrants Association of Serbia. He was my friend. But that has nothing to do with his alleged activities that he allegedly engaged in arms trafficking, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you drove Brana Crncevic to my house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 179, let me tell you that Brana Crncevic was never in my house, never.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Is your house, Mr. Milosevic, across the road to the former president of Yugoslavia, that writer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He is in a different street. Quite close by, but in a different street that is at right angles to my own street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, very close. I know I drove him to your place. He told me that I was driving him to his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that he could have said that, because he never went to my house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: So you never had whisky together?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We certainly did, but not in my house. Brana Crncevic was never in my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard that. We've heard the witness's response. He says that he took this man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is an absolute falsehood. Brana Crncevic was never in my house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You said that whatever I said was not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sometimes you must understand that constant repetition of a point doesn't improve it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. What then can I say about this allegation: Slobodan Milosevic, Jovica Stanisic, Brana Crncevic, and Mihalj Kertes and some others usually met in the morning at the premises of the state security and discussed deliveries to the SAO Krajina and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, I'm being accused here as an autocratic ruler that everyone came to consult. I don't see how now you should give a completely different impression. Can you imagine me beginning my working day by going to the state security service to meet with various people in that service, and then I go to my own office? Don't you understand how nonsensical that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I certainly didn't make your own timetable. I'm saying what I heard about meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That I first go in the morning to the security service and then to my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, not every morning but occasionally. I didn't say you went there every morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Meetings in the state security service could be attended by people working in that service and not by someone else. What would Brana Crncevic and Mihalj Kertes be doing there, not to mention me? Where did you get that idea from? Who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, I was in the state security at MUP Serbia on one occasion with Mihalj Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you there perhaps when I was attending a meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. I heard that from Milan Prodanic, your man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You heard that from someone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Not someone, from Milan Prodanic, head of the 6th department of the state security of the MUP of Serbia. Maybe you're going to tell us that you don't know him or that he doesn't know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do I know who Milan Prodanic knows and who knows Milan Prodanic? I am telling you that this is absurd when you say that I, in the morning, go to these premises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made that point, and the witness has given his answer, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear up a few more matters, please. You say that you met with Radovan Karadzic in a rather strange manner. Actually, it is true that not once but several times that we from Serbia did send humanitarian convoys to the citizens of Sarajevo on a non-discriminatory basis, which means to both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. You're aware of that, I assume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I led the first convoy that went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The first convoy. I see. So then you know that Serbia sent a convoy to the citizens of Sarajevo, both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, from what you say, it emerges that the convoy was stopped or, rather, that Karadzic met with you to stop the humanitarian aid and then that you demanded of Karadzic that the very next day he should remove obstacles and barriers and patrols from the roads, and then he got scared and removed them and allowed you to go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It's beautiful really the way you've interpreted this. Let me put it in a slightly different way. This aid from the government of Serbia, a part was for Pale and the second part for Sarajevo. When I arrived at Pale, the first thing that I was told was to go to Karadzic's villa for dinner. I sent some of my men to that dinner, but I stayed behind with two other men to secure the vehicles, and then later on I went to that villa too. And the first problem was that my men were disarmed at the entrance to this villa, and I was very angry, which that meant they didn't trust my men with weapons and they were armed, which meant that I didn't trust those men either. Biljana Plavsic was there with her sister. She knew me. And then she asked me to wait until she went to see Karadzic. She went to see him, and then he invited me to come upstairs to his office. I went there. They required that all the humanitarian aid be unloaded at Pale. There was a debate, quite a fervent one. Four trucks of that convoy were supposed to go to Sarajevo. At first, he wouldn't allow those trucks to go to Sarajevo, and then he called up someone -- no, not someone, Djuretic. He was one of the assistants for Serbs outside Serbia. And I knew Djuretic personally. He asked Karadzic on the phone who was there, and he told him my first and last name, and then Karadzic gave in and allowed those four trucks to leave for Sarajevo. At great difficulty and in spite of heavy fighting on the Sarajevo airstrip, I managed to reach Sarajevo without any serious problems. I reached the police station at Ilidza. I couldn't go any further, and those four trucks were unloaded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 179, without offence, I have no intention of insulting you. My questions are based on what you wrote in your statement. So let me remind you what you wrote in your statement on page 5. I think you have that statement in front of you. This is in paragraph 15, which is quite a long one. I won't read it all. "The aid was meant for all ethnic groups, not only Serbs. I stopped in Pale and had a meeting with Radovan Karadzic who wanted to stop me from going to Sarajevo. He wanted me to hand over that aid to the Red Cross in Pale. I knew his wife was the president of the Red Cross in Pale, and I also knew that they used to sell the humanitarian aid they received in the warehouses. I told him that I would leave for Sarajevo the next morning and that he should remove his patrols from the road because I would shoot if I saw anybody in uniform." So you went to Karadzic who wanted to keep the humanitarian aid. You threatened to shoot, and then they got scared and removed everything, and you were able to reach Sarajevo. Isn't that right what emerges from this paragraph? You say: "I managed to deliver the aid in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. I said that I would shoot if anyone stood in my way. Don't believe that I'm lying. I know very well what I was doing and what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness 179, I'm just quoting what you said. "To remove patrols from the roads because I would shoot if I saw anybody in uniform."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. If he stood in my way, I would shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in the face of such a threat of yours, they let you go on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was because of this threat or because of the conversation with Djuretic from the Ministry for Serbs outside Serbia, but I said what I said and I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any document whereby Brana Crncevic, as president of the Emigrants Association, or anyone on -- anyone else on his behalf signed any kind of permission or authorisation for the transportation of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Brana Crncevic did not, but I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You signed on behalf of the Brana Crncevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, in my own name but on behalf of the Association of Serbs. That was my part -- a part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to show me what it is that you signed on behalf of the Association of Serbs. I see tab 11 here. Four automatic rifles, two pistols, two automatic pistols. This is linked to the request that we quoted from a moment ago; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, but there are other requests too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document which seems to be a photocopy, Mr. Kwon, and which has the number ERN 03269340, it is a handwritten document. Under number 1 is an automatic rifle, 7.62, four pieces. And then a 7.62 pistol, semi-automatic, 2. Then a pistol 7.62, automatic 2, and then the rest has to do with bullets or rounds. That is what is linked to this letter of Brana Crncevic's where he says: "We request that for the needs of the Association of Serbs for the escort of the transport and its security you issue the following," and we see that less was issued than requested. And it says: MORS, which I assume, means the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but English translation says the number of quantity of pistols at 12. Whether OTP can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I hope that you yourself, regardless of the fact that this document is in Serbian, you can see the numbers in column number 5, and the heading for that column is "Quantity" and the numbers are indicated by hand, 422, and then the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, how they translated that, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, perhaps you'd look into that. It does seem to be inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would concede that it does appear to be to somebody misread the way the person made the 2 as really being a one and a two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we need a new translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then the other receipts, the one with the ERN 341, ending with 341, refers to six rifles, then the other one two rifles, and then when you add all that up, it roughly amounts to what you requested. On the back side of this receipt, I assume, are the names of the people to whom these weapons were issued, and I suppose the serial numbers of those weapons. Is that right, Mr. 179? It's just one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is some difficulty about the interpreters hearing. Can we start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying, Mr. May, that in tab 10 is the letter from Brana Crncevic requesting these 15 rifles and eight pistols for the escorts and security of a convoy, and this was addressed to the Ministry of Defence. And then in tab 11, we have the receipts whereby those weapons were issued. On the first one, four plus two plus two; on the second receipt six rifles; and on the third receipt two; which means a total of 12. One could add up the other items, but all this fits within the context of this letter requesting weapons for the escort and security of a convoy, and it all amounts to some 15 weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. That's your interpretation. Let the witness answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, it is true that that was requested of the Ministry of Defence, but also there are many, many things whereby the Ministry of Defence was sidestepped, has nothing to do with the Ministry of Defence. You just read out what is there, but I have many more such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to tab 11. I was going from one document to the next. I can't read what I don't have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Milosevic, I have a permit to carry weapons and ammunition which doesn't exist among these documents, and I have a licence signed by Bora Stanisic for a M-84 machine-gun, a heavy machine-gun. You won't find that weapon anywhere here. Then I have a licence for a pistol, CZ-799. Also you won't find that in these documents. What I'm trying to say is something else: There were documents, these minor quantities, to account for them, but for the others, you won't find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. 179, to cover such vast quantities of weapons that you say you transported cannot be accounted for by this collection of receipts which, when added up, amounts to 12 or 15 pieces of weaponry. Surely this request of Brana Crncevic asking for some weapons for the security of the transport and your own personal safety cannot account for that large quantity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that applies to only that part of the weaponry. I had a far larger number of documents. I don't know whether you know that you searched my house, looking through my dirty linen and everything else, and that you seized a good number of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, I heard of you for the first time and saw you for the first time today, and be sure that I did not search your house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: But people from the state security did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how an apartment can be searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I do know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There has to be a judicial order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have to break there. Mr. Milosevic, you will have ten minutes left. We will go into private session to deal with an administrative matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are in open session. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I cannot finish the examination of this witness within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, do what you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, please give me brief answers to my questions. In paragraph 8, you said that the military equipment came from military post code 5055 in Bubanj Potok which was the storage facility of the command of the town of Belgrade, city of Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I really have a problem. I'm receiving the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that the military equipment came from military post code 5055 in Bubanj Potok, which was the storage facility of the command of the city of Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any proof that a certain type or amount of weapons from this source was delivered, as you claimed, through the matica to the Krajina or Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I have travel authorisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see among your papers here, the ones accompanying your statement, a shred of evidence to support this claim of yours, so I'm asking you whether you do have any proof.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I do have proof. You saw from the approval of the Ministry of Defence itself. You see that there is only one document concerning the giving of weapons to the matica for meeting the needs of our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the evidence that we already discussed, and that is a set of receipts issued for purposes of providing security for transports on the basis of an order that is -- and the number is on each and every one of them. That is 332/2, dated the 20th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is that the only proof that you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. There's also Gabos concerning the 82-millimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you say that you have this evidence concerning 82-millimetre mortar shells --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, please -- take that document, then. That is a page ending with the numbers 8383. You say that you personally received these mortar shells, the ones that are specified in this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you receive them from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, you see, at that time it was not allowed to have people sign, those who gave them to you. It was Boro Stanisic who gave them to me, but it does give the number, the military post code number 5055.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see here, please look at 8, 9, 10, items 8, 9, 10 on this document. Tell me, which weapons were issued, who is the order issuing authority? Who received this? All of these spaces are empty, Mr. 179?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. Mr. Milosevic and the witness are talking about two different documents. The document Mr. Milosevic has referred the witness to is tab number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Item number 8, handed over. Number 9, received; 10, order issuing authority. And the space there is empty, all three boxes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It is correct all three spaces are empty, because no signatures were placed there. That was the beginning when the war had just started, but the receipt was issued by military post 5055 and, also, there is the stamp of the matica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The stamp that you placed and your signature. But as opposed to the other receipts where persons signed their names, those who issued orders, who received this, who handed it over, and also mention is made of the order that is relevant. Here all these spaces are empty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Well, this proves that I am one of the people who did not exist at that time of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 179, this proves that that is a forgery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. No. I never forged any such thing, nor did any such thing ever cross my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we agree at least that here in the spaces assigned for "issued by," "received by," "ordered by," there is nothing written in these boxes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: We can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the document whose ERN number ends in 385. This is a receipt too. Is it clear that what is written here, "Rifles are taken over and returned --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says -- it says, "Received, handed over, and order issuing authority."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can help, this is tab 11, the one but last receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Issued by," "received by," "ordered by," all of it is written, and it also says that the weapons are taken over and returned to Bubanj Potok for the needs of the convoy of the government of the Republic of Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it says on this document, like on the others, that for the weapons received, they should, rather, be returned to Bubanj Potok and that this is for the needs of the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these weapons also issued on the basis of document 3/132/2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly, but I doubt it. I doubt it, because a great many weapons were issued while the Ministry of Defence was sidestepped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But on the receipt it says KOGB, and the number is number 3/132/2. All of this pertains to the weapons that were requested for providing security for the convoy. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. 179?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: All the receipts that were issued by the command of the city of Belgrade have this designation KOGB, and also at the request of the government of the Republic of Serbia. However, as far as I know, the ministry of the Republic of Serbia, the Ministry of Defence did not take part in this, and they could not have known about this because this was known by a very small circle of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so the Ministry of Defence did not know about this? Only you knew about it and a few other people, and me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, very well. But you don't have a shred of evidence for that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You will receive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now is the time for you to provide this proof because you are testifying now. Tell me now, you also gave a letter here addressed to the Association of Emigres - 0290873 is the ERN number - and the head from Donji Lapac, a certain Dusko Vojvodic, is sending this, and he is asking for some military equipment from the Association of Emigres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the appropriate tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's tab 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Uniforms, blankets, automatic rifles and the rest are requested here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, in addition to the Association of Emigrants, is any other state authority mentioned here, either of Yugoslavia or of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No. No one is mentioned here, but it is well known. This came to the Association of Emigrants, to Brana Crncevic. He gave me this document, and with this document I went over to Bubanj Potok, and I handed it over to Bora Stanisic. Bora Stanisic handed this over to Milan Prodanic, and then decisions were made as to where things would be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. Do you have any evidence that the matica addressed the JNA or the Territorial Defence of Serbia or the Ministry of Defence in relation to this request? So the matica is requesting weapons for providing security for the convoy, and they are not sending a request in relation to this; is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm claiming. I've been telling you all the time that the Ministry of Defence was sidestepped. Very few people knew about these supplies and these convoys, and it's impossible that you did not know what the state security of the MUP of Serbia was doing, Jovica Stanisic and Prodanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You do not have a single document to prove this. I'm asking you - so I'm not going to claim anything - can you show a document which confirms that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All of this argument. You're arguing with the witness again, wasting time. He gives his evidence. He's not to be argued with. Now, you can ask him about the document, of course, but that's as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not arguing. I'm not arguing, Mr. May. I am asking the witness whether he can show me any document confirming whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is the matter of argument. He's produced the documents he has. It is for you to ask him about it. There's no need to argue with him further when he has produced here what he has.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, isn't it clear that this kind of request could have lost its way and reached the matica? It's not that that the matica had any weapons at their disposal. That's why I'm asking the witness whether he had any document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has told you that the matica was distributing the weapons. You dispute that, and so there is really very little point in going on and arguing about it. He has given his evidence quite plainly. Here was the matica distributing weapons all over Croatia and Bosnia. You say that's not true. We will have to make our minds up where the truth lies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify the following point: You claim that the matica did not address itself to the government or other official authorities, but that they directly took weapons from the 5055 storage facility and that they were allowed to do so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You also claim that the command of the military post also issued weapons and military equipment to the matica without any kind of certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Not to the Matica. They gave it to me, and I took it further on to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any kind of certificate to prove that? So it was issued to you without a certificate? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have travel authorisations here, and I also have work authorisations here and you can also see that they bear the stamps of 1055 here and of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbia and the stamps of the matica, the Association of Emigrants of Serbia, and I drove vehicles with weapons of the -- with the registration plates of the Yugoslav People's Army and military licence plates, civilian licence plates, and you cannot tell me that this is not correct when this is correct, and everybody knows that full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your travel authorisations now. Does that prove that you carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: In the travel authorisation, there are also -- there are only the numbers of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Numbers of vehicles. And then you were allowed to be involved in transport, and you transported humanitarian aid of the Matica of Emigrants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that the Association of Emigrants did not have weapons but humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: And then why would the matica use registration plates of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Association of Emigrants, as far as I know, begged everybody for assistance in terms of transportation vehicles for transporting humanitarian aid. Everybody, private owners, the army, state organs, economic organisations, because they themselves did not have any such thing. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, it's not right, Mr. Milosevic. Precisely from the matica a MAN trailer truck went that belonged to the Bugojno forwarding company of the MUP of Serbia and I precisely gave this vehicle that was used by the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say, the state security for transporting military equipment and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what you say, Mr. 179, because you said that on the basis of this order 3/132/2 -- do you at least have that order on the basis of which these weapons were being issued and this would cast more light on the nature of the receipts that you provided here, and then we could perhaps establish what all of this is about, because so far we've established only that these were rifles for providing security for convoys, and that's the only thing that's registered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Milosevic, that's what you allege. We've heard the witness's evidence as to what it was that was being transported, but you've got -- we'll allow you two more questions. You've already had over the time which we allotted. Now, two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Then I'll put this question: To whom did you deliver, since you say you were delivering weapons to Zvecevo, to whom did you deliver them in Zvecevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was -- whether he was a lieutenant colonel or colonel, I'm not sure, but he was from the Novi Sad Corps who had come to Zvecevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Tell me one more thing. You state that you had carried money from the Topcider mint to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it at the time when the dinar of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was introduced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean, then, that the mint of the National Bank of Yugoslavia at Topcider provided services for the needs of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I don't know whether they provided services. All I know is that I was ordered to load up the money and carry it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To whom did you deliver the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't know. I know Jova Danilovic drove the truck with the money. I only added one padlock to avoid possible problems. He delivered to somebody in Knin. To whom exactly, I don't know. All I know is that there was another amount of money with foreign currencies loaded up there and carried back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that money? Who handed it over to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Nobody handed it to me. They handed it to my driver. My driver signed for it, that he received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he sign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: He signed that he received banknotes for Knin, a full truckload, seven to eight tons of dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the Republic of Serbian Krajina. 1 A. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So money intended for the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. The money printed in Topcider.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the driver went alone. You didn't go with him and you don't know to whom he handed it over.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I didn't accompany him to the mint at Topcider, but I led that convoy up to Knin, and then to whom he handed over that money in Knin, I don't know, because it was his job to hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you led the convoy, but you don't know to whom the money was handed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I don't know. To somebody at the bank there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered as best he can. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to go back to this topic from paragraph 21 of your statement regarding this money. If you would be kind enough to look at your statement. You said in the first sentence: "I remember that on one occasion I transported a whole truckload of RSK dinars to Knin. This must have been seven to eight tons of freshly printed RSK dinars." So you say that you drove that money personally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then a couple of sentences on, you say: "I was the first one to deliver RSK dinars to Knin." And then: "I do not know why these deliveries took place, because I was just the driver. I do not remember to whom I delivered the money." Whereas here you -- here in the statement you said that you drove and you handed it over. How do you explain the discrepancy between this and what you said just a second ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: There is a slight error here. I'm telling you that the money was taken there by the truck driver Jovo Danilovic and I was the one leading the convoy. There was always a leader of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you delivered the money. If you had delivered the money and you are denying it now, there must be a document to prove it, because it's a huge amount of money, and then a huge amount of foreign currency was taken back. Is there a document to prove that this amount of money - because it's huge - was taken and handed over there? Do you have that document or does somebody else have it, somebody who drove the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It was signed by Jovo Danilovic, because he would take it to Knin and he would leave the document to Belgrade on his way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then I have a couple of more questions about this set of documents under tab 9. We see here an authorisation from which it is evident that you took over a truck, a bus, and it says that this vehicle would be (redacted) .

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone able to drive a vehicle that didn't belong to them without having an authorisation, a document? I'm not talking about arms deliveries, I'm talking about driving regulations because of routine controls. Did you have to have an authorisation as somebody who was not the owner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you have an authorisation for every vehicle allowing you to drive it, because it didn't belong to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I'll give you an example of this bus precisely. This bus came from Vukovar, and I got this pass because I was the only one who had the licence to drive the bus, and I used this bus to drive refugees to their destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that earlier. I wouldn't like to come back to that. Let us just discuss the document from tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've requested a redaction be made, but may I remind Mr. Tapuskovic not to mention the witness's name on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's at line 13:10:47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mentioned the driver's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but only as a driver. I didn't mention his name and surname. I can't understand. I can't explain this error. I don't believe I made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in this tab 10 we discussed already that the weapons that were requested were requested for purposes of security of convoys and all these documents under tab 11 concern precisely those weapons requested for security details for convoys and drivers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I will try to give you a more detailed explanation now. When we drove military convoys, we did not need any authorisations. Civilian transports were another matter. When you were transporting civilians or civilian property, it was a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why am I asking you this? You said you led three convoys plus one in relation to those besieged Serbs. There were three or four convoys.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: There were some more, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It does matter, Witness, because if you look at paragraph 15 -- no, paragraph 7, you say: "While I was," this and that, "the unit transported more than 1.200 truckloads of ammunition and weapons that had been taken from Bubanj Potok." Then a couple of sentences down, you say: "I know this personally because I participated myself in the transport." This is mentioned after your reference to 1.200 trucks. How do you explain this if you were involved in only three or four convoys?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You're trying to set a trap for me. I said something entirely different. I said that in 1992, 1.200 trucks were transported from Bubanj Potok, carrying ammunition and weapons. And I said vehicles from the Association of Emigrants were involved but also vehicles from the MUP of Serbia and other civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look now at paragraph 17. You say: "When these weapons were transported, the receivers of the arms had to sign for it when we delivered it. When I picked up the weapons in Bubanj Potok -" and you say when - "I was always given the name of the receiving party. I think I will be able to find the receipt for the weapons, and I will contact the investigator when I do." That is something you say in the statement drawn up in March this year. You cannot mention any contact related to the weapons received in Krajina or in Bosnia by the Serbs from these areas.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You are very wrong, Mr. Tapuskovic. I had major problems. My family received threats in this period. From my first contact with the Hague Tribunal, I received an anonymous call telling me that I would be killed. I had to hide my family away because we were receiving threats. Every night telephones would ring and the caller would ring off immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not without reason.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Let me tell you my story to the end. You will receive these documents. I will find them. Part of these documents are still in existence. I kept documents in various places. I had to conceal a part of them, but I was not able to collect them before my travel to The Hague, but I will pick them up, and I will bring them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. But today in response to different questions, you already answered that you do not have these documents because everything was burnt in your home, and on another occasion you said that everything had been removed from your apartment. How can you produce them if you don't have them any more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: You are wrong, Mr. Tapuskovic. I said the documentation from the military base 5055 had been burnt. It wasn't burnt in my apartment. And it was during searches of my apartment that a part of my documentation was removed. I said it loud and clear. Please do not try to confuse these two things. Nothing in my house was burnt. It was the documentation of military base 5055 that was burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. You mentioned today for the first time that you met Mladic, Krajisnik, Tepavcevic, Lajnovic, Buca, Brka, Isidor and other people, and you never mentioned before that you had any meetings, any encounters with the people you mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I don't know what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you met Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you hadn't mentioned it before. The same goes for Mladic. You mentioned the paramilitaries of Lajnovic and Tepavcevic and you had not mentioned any of these persons before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: I will try to give you an explanation of this. When I gave my first statement in Belgrade, it was in the offices of the ICTY, precisely at the time when the Prime Minister of Serbia was killed. And my meeting there was cut short, and I got my first opportunity to explain certain things when I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the Judges was interested in this topic that I'm going to cover now. You say that somebody conveyed certain information to Slobodan Milosevic, but here in paragraph 11, you already spoke about this, and you said in no unclear terms that Slobodan Milosevic talked every morning with the persons you mention here about arms deliveries to Krajina. If he participated directly in these discussions, why would he need to be informed about them? Can you explain this for the benefit of the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes, I can very easily explain. I said that he did not always attend. He sometimes attended, and on other occasions he was briefed. I think he was perfectly clear on this, and you are confusing things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one document that I would ask to be added to the binder of exhibits to be used with this witness, and I'd ask that the witness be shown this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, that is document containing two identification cards. I'd like to draw your attention to the identification card on the lower part of the document. Sir, whose identification card is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: That is an identity card of the Association of Serbian Emigrants concerning assistance to Serbian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that your identification card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at the second page which is a copy of the reverse of that card. Does that bear your name and the stamp of the association?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. We can see my name here and the stamp of the association and my personal identity card number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that under seal, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that will be tab 14.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 14, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. B-179, what is your base of knowledge when you say that more than 1.200 trucks of ammunition had been transported? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It is based on the conversations between Bora Stanisic and Milan Prodanic that I overheard that took place in Bubanj Potok when they were saying that we had managed to transport over 1.200 trucks full of ammunition and weapons with great success to Republika Srpska and the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell me when it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: It was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just in relation to this document that Mr. Groome introduced a minute ago, since it wasn't introduced before my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are two documents here, actually. I suppose that the witness can see that, because he received this a couple of seconds before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the first document is a copy of his personal identity card, the kind that every citizen of Yugoslavia has?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we see here that this identity card was issued in December 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the time that you are testifying about; is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I changed my identity card. The identity card that I had was taken by the office of the ICTY when I was giving my statement. That is why these don't correspond. My old card and my new card. They made a photocopy of my new card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Leaving that aside, I only want to note that this first document is a copy of the personal identity card issued in December 2000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: Yes. And it bears a different identity card number. If you would be kind to look at it, it says M -- registration number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Now, what is the point of this? The accused points out accurately it's dated 2000. We waste time in this case in this sort of way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution isn't offering or isn't tendering the top document. The Prosecution is only tendering the image on the bottom half of this page, which is the identification card for the association which the accused has alleged he never held the position in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. No. We're going to bring this to an end. You wanted to say something, Mr. Witness. Did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. I just want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to bring this to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us clear up this second matter too, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This second ID card has on it the Matica of Serbs and Emigrants of Serbia, with a photograph, which is quite unclear, and below that it says "aid to Serbian refugees." That is what it says. And on this other page, on the reverse side, it says the name and last name of this witness. So the entire document only relates to the fact that it is the Matica of Emigrants of Serbia and Serb Refugees, and the name of the witness with a number that I am not familiar with, and it does not coincide at all with the other number in the other document. So it says nothing else. That's all that is said in this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-179
utterances.text: May I clarify? On the reverse side of this ID card is my ID card number while I was working in the matica. So this is the old ID card number. An ID lasts ten years. I had to change it because it had expired. And that is why the number of the ID card on the upper document does not coincide with the number on the reverse side of the other document. Mr. Milosevic must know this very well. He's just pretending not to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to pursue this any further. The issue, in any event, has not been whether the -- whether there was any involvement with the matica. The role has been the role of that association -- the issue has been the role of that association. We really must bring these matters to an end. Witness B-179, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. But just wait, if you would, until we've pulled down the blinds, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection regarding you personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You can make an objection -- you can make an objection to some part of the evidence, but you can't make an objection to me personally. Now, what is the objection you want to make?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that you're allowing this witness to use a rather common language which is not appropriate for civilised behaviour, rather crude language used on several occasions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Such crude language as there may have been has not been interpreted, so we've not been able to follow it. If there had been an objection earlier, we would have dealt with it. Yes. Thank you, B-179, if you'd like to go now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the changeover of witnesses, can I use the time for two very short administrative matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to go, Mr. B-179.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, we've reviewed the position about the witness Harland in light of the amicus objections to the document or a substantial part of it being subject to 92 bis. We think there's force in their argument and that what would be left to be 92 bis is really not worth troubling you with, and therefore in reality we think that the whole of the evidence should be given viva voce and we shouldn't trouble you further. I'm sorry to have taken your time thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, a sensible concession if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second thing is the lists on witnesses need not be prepared because there is not real prospect of there being time to call them are in preparation. I hope to have the lists to you by the end of business today, courtesy copy or otherwise, and I hope that will be helpful to cover both list A and the 92 bis witnesses, although I think there may be yet further names on the Bosnia 92 bis list whom we will be able to suggest later on needn't be subject to preparation, but we're doing out best to minimise preparatory work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It might be helpful, speaking for myself, if we could simply have a list of those witnesses in addition of the witnesses who you intend to call between now and the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It's of course to be found on list A, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I know, but I have to say for myself I find it confusing because in it there are all the witnesses you have called.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We did that intentionally so that you could have a continuing document, but if you find it more helpful we can simply strip out and republish with all those names deleted, leaving the numbers for the witnesses frozen at what they were for ease of reference amongst yourselves or with your legal others or with us. I'll have that dealt with in one way or another today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If would you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We are also hoping to get to you today a filing on the witness list, deletions and additions that I hope will basically take us to the end of the case subject to other eventualities. But Mr. Ierace will be taking the next witness, and I'll hand it over to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness will take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you Aernout van Lynden, Baron Aernout van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am.
