utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm currently working as a lecturer at the American university in Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were you previously, for some 22 years, a war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of the witness's testimony in the Galic trial has been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis (D). Some further material has been admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis (A). I will present a summary of combined evidence. Some matters which do not qualify for admission under those rules will be the subject of viva voce evidence. Four brief news stories or parts thereof which were filed by this witness will also be shown. In relation to the witness's background, Baron van Lynden, a Dutch national was born in London in 1954 and was educated in the United Kingdom. As a -- he was a war correspondent who covered the Yugoslavian conflict for Sky News, a satellite news service including Croatia in 1991 from the Serb side and the siege of Sarajevo. He had previously covered the war in Lebanon, the Iraq-Iran war from both sides, and the Gulf War. Prior to becoming a war correspondent in 1978, he was an officer in the Dutch Marine Corps, specialising in mortars. He stayed in Sarajevo on the Bosnian side between May and August 1992. In September 1992, with the assistance of Dr. Karadzic, he spent three and a half weeks on the Bosnian Serb side. He was again in Sarajevo from the end of October until late December 1992. Thereafter, he visited Sarajevo sporadically for a few days at a time, except after the first market -- Markale market incident in 1994 when he stayed for a few weeks. In relation to the settlement of Dobrinja, he marked its position on a map as being to the west of the city alongside the airport and gave evidence that it was separately besieged, being cut off from the rest of Sarajevo until June 1992, when Bosnian forces took control of the nearby Mojmilo hill. In relation to the layout of Sarajevo generally, the witness has stated that it was an elongated city lying in a valley along the Miljaka River. The Bosnian Serb forces held the high ground and were able from those positions to fire along the streets which intersected the main east-west thoroughfare, Marsal Tito Boulevard. Accordingly, an alternative pedestrian route was developed to enable the inhabitants to traverse the city along the valley floor on an east-west access, in particular at the valley's narrowest point which was the central city area in the vicinity of Marin Dvor and the Marsal Tito barracks where the Bosnian held part of the valley floor was about a kilometre wide and immediately adjacent to the Bosnian Serb-held Grbavica. This route involved utilising building cover and anti-sniping barricades and has been indicated on a map which is Annex II to the witness's 92 bis statement. The witness has given evidence that whilst residing on the Bosnian Serb side in September 1992, with the permission of General Mladic, his Sky News team spent ten days touring various Bosnian Serb front-line positions around Sarajevo, escorted by two Bosnian Serb military policemen. As they did so, the witness was introduced to the various company commanders. These officers wore their JNA uniforms displaying their JNA ranks, having changed their badges from the JNA to the Bosnian Serb army. During this tour, he noticed that the Bosnian Serb gunners from their commanding positions were able to personally sight their targets rather than rely on observers, thereby enabling more accurate fire. The topography also allowed relatively few infantry forces backed up by artillery to keep large numbers of Bosnian troops committed to the defence of Sarajevo. At Grbavica along the Miljaka River which delineated the opposing forces at that point, he was shown several sandbagged positions in apartment blocks operated by uniformed soldiers armed with machine-guns and what he recognised to be sniping rifles and in radio communication case with spotters who apparently assisted them to locate targets. In one fourth-floor position they utilised a dummy decoy. Elsewhere in Bosnian Serb held Grbavica he saw mortars, tanks, armoured personnel carriers, which are known as APCs, and vehicle-mounted anti-aircraft artillery. The state hospital. The witness described the state hospital as being positioned in front of Marin Dvor square as were the Bosnian Parliament Buildings and in a direct line of site and fire from the Bosnian Serb forces in Grbavica. His news team stayed there from May to August 1992, camping in the shelled out upper floors because it gave them an ideal filming position of the city and the surrounding hills which were occupied by the Bosnian Serb forces. The hospital continued to function from the lower levels. From there, in the four days and nights following the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks in June 1992, they filmed the city being shelled indiscriminately from Bosnian Serb positions. He estimated that over a thousand shells from heavy weapons including anti-aircraft artillery fell on the city each night. All tracer rounds were seen coming into the city. The witness contrasted the saturated fire which was concentrated on the Marsal Tito barracks following its evacuation with indiscriminate fire where shells would land randomly all over Sarajevo. In his opinion, this random fire was directed at the city generally and those who lived in it. Its effect was inculcate fear in the city's inhabitants. In this period during these four days and nights, he observed the Unis towers which were twin commercial towers of 35 to 40 storeys high near Marin Dvor square being almost completely destroyed by Bosnian Serb shelling even though up until that time they had not been a source of fire by Bosnian forces. He witnessed a steady stream of casualties coming into the state hospital, filling the emergency ward and corridors. During his stays and visits to Sarajevo during the war, the witness observed other instances of deliberate attack of civilians and civilian facilities by Bosnian Serb forces. In mid-July 1992, he witnessed a sniping incident. At about 4.00 p.m. on Marsal Tito Boulevard, he observed two men and a woman dressed in civilian clothes lying on the ground in place which was open to Bosnian Serb positions. The woman wore a skirt and had with her what appeared to be a shopping bag. All three people appeared to be in their 40s and had been shot. Two were moaning. He was told by bystanders that initially one was shot, then a person who went to assist, and finally a third person who went to assist those two. The witness observed a Bosnian APC arrive, but before it could provide cover to the three adults, at least two single shots struck them. The two men were killed. He does not recall whether the woman survived. The second incident concerned an apartment block shelling. On the 5th of December, 1992, while driving along Marsal Tito Boulevard, the Sky News team observed a high-rise apartment block near the road which accommodated several hundred people, including children, being hit with incendiary rounds that were coming from the direction of the nearest Bosnian Serb positions, which were to the south of the Miljaka River. They stopped and filmed the incident and spoke to the residents, determining that the building had not been used by the defending military forces according to the residents and, therefore, in the witness's opinion, was not a military target. While the fire department attempted to put out the ensuing fire, the building continued to receive incendiary rounds at levels lower than the firefighters. While driving on the Bosnian side, the witness observed that mortars would on occasion land either in front of his vehicle or behind his vehicle, leading him to conclude that his vehicle was being sniped, so as to speak, by Bosnian Serb mortar crews. In relation to the Jewish cemetery, on two occasions the witness visited the positions of Bosnian Serb forces in the area of the Jewish cemetery, which was positioned on the confrontation lines and overlooked the southern part of the city, in particular, Marin Dvor. On one visit in February 1994, he met the local commander, a person known as Aleksic. He observed that his troops were not uniformed and were armed with non-standard weaponry. He was informed, that is the witness, was informed by his Bosnian Serb minder who accompanied him from the Pale headquarters that Aleksic and his men nevertheless came under the command of the local Bosnian Serb army commander. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prior to the first Markale market incident which was on the 5th of February, 1994, it was not possible to cross Marin Dvor square safely, the witness said in his evidence, since it attracted fire from Bosnian Serb forces on an almost daily basis. The fact that it was possible to walk across it in March 1994 during the cease-fire which immediately followed the Markale market incident confirmed to the witness that Aleksic was indeed subject to a centralised command and control system. In relation to the Bosnian army, the witness observed that the Bosnian army in the city had significantly less weaponry than did the Bosnian Serb forces. He had seen a tank on the Bosnian army side, and in February 1994, at a weapon collection point set up in the city, he saw 120-millimetre mortars but no artillery. He observed that the Bosnian army was multi-ethnic in its composition, including people who were identified as being Serbian or Croatian as well as of the Muslim faith. In the early stages of the conflict, he noted that the Bosnian army was not consistently outfitted in uniforms. In mid-1992, he met a Bosnian paramilitary by the name of Juka Prazina who the witness estimated had 200 to 300 men under his command. They were armed and un-uniformed except that they tended to wear black. As to military targets in the city, on occasion he would visit various Bosnian army officers which were located in what as far as he could tell had previously been non-military office buildings. On one occasion he saw a mortar that had been set up in the grounds of Kosevo Hospital. As to conditions in the city by May 1992, the shops were empty and food had to be brought in. Some tried to grow vegetables for themselves, but many lived in apartment blocks and, therefore, were unable to do so. When on the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation lines, in particular in the area of Grbavica, the witness had observed anti-sniping barricades, and he was informed that civilians on that side were being shot by snipers from the Bosnian side of the confrontation lines. He asked to be taken to the hospitals to see the victims but was not taken. As to prisons on the Bosnian side, the witness was aware of the existence of prisons in Sarajevo. He asked the Bosnian authorities for access to those prisons but was never given access. Your Honour, that concludes the presentation of the summary of the evidence. At this point I would show -- seek to show four video clips or some parts, but I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be a convenient moment to stop for the day. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes. Baron, could you remember, please, not speak to anybody about your evidence, not that you've given any so far, until it is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did I say 20 minutes? Adjourned for the day.
